items.meaning: A common way to ask if someone is available to meet or do something.
items.example: Are you free next Saturday evening? I'm planning a small dinner party.
items.plain: Can you meet next Saturday evening? I'm planning a small dinner party.
items.note: A direct and common way to check availability. Can be followed by a specific time or day.

items.meaning: Used to suggest an activity or a time to meet.
items.example: How about we grab a coffee sometime next week to discuss the project?
items.plain: Shall we grab a coffee sometime next week to discuss the project?
items.note: Versatile for suggesting times, activities, or people. Informal and friendly.

items.meaning: An informal way to ask what someone is doing or planning, often as a lead-in to an invitation.
items.example: Hey, what are you up to this weekend? I was thinking of going hiking.
items.plain: Hey, what are your plans for this weekend? I was thinking of going hiking.
items.note: Very common informal greeting among friends. Can be used to initiate plans.

items.meaning: An informal British English way to suggest an activity.
items.example: Fancy doing something fun tonight? There's a new exhibition opening.
items.plain: Would you like to do something fun tonight? There's a new exhibition opening.
items.note: Primarily British English. Very informal and friendly.

items.meaning: Suggestion to meet and talk about recent events in each other's lives.
items.example: It's been too long, let's catch up properly over dinner soon.
items.plain: It's been too long, let's meet and talk about our lives over dinner soon.
items.note: Very common and friendly. Implies a desire for a longer, more personal conversation.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask someone to suggest a convenient time to meet.
items.example: I'd love to meet up. When works for you next week?
items.plain: I'd love to meet up. What time is convenient for you next week?
items.note: Flexible and considerate, putting the choice of time on the other person.

items.meaning: To be busy and unavailable for a specific period.
items.example: I'm afraid I can't make it on Tuesday, I'm tied up with work commitments.
items.plain: I'm afraid I can't make it on Tuesday, I'm busy with work commitments.
items.note: Common and polite way to decline an invitation due to being busy.

items.meaning: To make a tentative arrangement or booking.
items.example: I'm not 100% sure yet, but you can pencil me in for the barbecue.
items.plain: I'm not 100% sure yet, but you can tentatively include me for the barbecue.
items.note: Implies a flexible commitment that might change. Informal.

items.meaning: To decline an invitation but suggest doing it another time.
items.example: I'm swamped this week, so I'll have to take a rain check on dinner.
items.plain: I'm swamped this week, so I'll have to decline dinner but suggest we do it another time.
items.note: A polite way to decline without closing the door on future plans.

items.meaning: A polite way to invite someone to do something.
items.example: Would you like to come over for a board game night next Friday?
items.plain: Do you want to come over for a board game night next Friday?
items.note: Standard, polite invitation. Can be used in various contexts.

items.meaning: To visit someone's home.
items.example: Why don't you come over for a casual dinner this weekend?
items.plain: Why don't you visit my home for a casual dinner this weekend?
items.note: Informal and friendly, used when inviting someone to your place.

items.meaning: A polite and open invitation, indicating permission or encouragement.
items.example: You're welcome to bring a friend along if you'd like to the party.
items.plain: You can bring a friend along if you'd like to the party.
items.note: Very hospitable. Often used to offer options or extend an invitation.

items.meaning: An invitation to participate in an activity or meal with a group.
items.example: We're going out for drinks after work, would you like to join us for a round?
items.plain: We're going out for drinks after work, would you like to come with us for a round?
items.note: Common for group activities. Friendly and inclusive.

items.meaning: A very enthusiastic and polite way to accept an invitation.
items.example: That sounds wonderful, I'd love to come to your housewarming party.
items.plain: That sounds wonderful, I would really like to come to your housewarming party.
items.note: Standard, warm acceptance. Can be used in almost any social context.

items.meaning: An enthusiastic and informal way to express approval or accept a suggestion.
items.example: A picnic in the park? Sounds great, I'll bring some snacks.
items.plain: A picnic in the park? That's a great idea, I'll bring some snacks.
items.note: Very common and versatile for expressing positive reception to an idea.

items.meaning: To confirm one's participation in an activity or event.
items.example: If you're planning a trip to the beach, count me in!
items.plain: If you're planning a trip to the beach, include me!
items.note: Informal and enthusiastic way to accept, often for group activities.

items.meaning: A very informal and quick way to accept an invitation or agree to participate.
items.example: A spontaneous road trip this weekend? I'm in!
items.plain: A spontaneous road trip this weekend? I'll participate!
items.note: Highly informal and enthusiastic. Used among close friends.

items.text: I'm afraid I can't make it
items.form: I'm afraid I can't make it
items.meaning: A polite and common way to decline an invitation.
items.example: Thank you for the invitation, but I'm afraid I can't make it to the concert.
items.plain: Thank you for the invitation, but I cannot come to the concert.
items.note: Standard, polite refusal. Often followed by a brief reason or apology.

items.meaning: To have a prior engagement or plan, making one unavailable.
items.example: I'd love to, but I've got something on that evening already.
items.plain: I'd love to, but I have a prior engagement that evening already.
items.note: A common and slightly vague way to decline without giving full details.

items.meaning: Used to suggest rescheduling or doing something at a later, unspecified date.
items.example: I'm really busy this week, but let's do it another time soon.
items.plain: I'm really busy this week, but let's do it at a different time soon.
items.note: Polite way to decline while keeping the possibility open for the future.

items.meaning: A casual and polite way to acknowledge an invitation, often when declining.
items.example: Thanks for the invite to your party, but I'm out of town that weekend.
items.plain: Thank you for inviting me to your party, but I'm out of town that weekend.
items.note: Informal and friendly. Can be used when accepting or declining.

items.meaning: An invitation to a guest to relax and feel comfortable in one's house.
items.example: Come in, come in! Make yourself at home, the kitchen is through there.
items.plain: Come in, come in! Feel comfortable and relaxed here, the kitchen is through there.
items.note: Standard phrase for welcoming guests. Very hospitable.

items.meaning: An invitation to a guest to take food or drink freely.
items.example: The drinks are in the fridge, so please help yourself to anything you like.
items.plain: The drinks are in the fridge, so please take anything you like.
items.note: Common and polite way to offer food/drink to guests.

items.meaning: A polite expression of gratitude to a host for their hospitality.
items.example: It was a lovely evening, thanks for having me over for dinner.
items.plain: It was a lovely evening, thank you for inviting me to your home for dinner.
items.note: Standard and polite phrase used by a guest when leaving or afterwards.

items.text: It was lovely to see you
items.form: It was lovely to see you
items.meaning: A warm and polite farewell phrase, expressing enjoyment of someone's company.
items.example: Well, I should get going. It was lovely to see you both!
items.plain: Well, I should get going. I enjoyed seeing you both!
items.note: Common and friendly closing remark when parting ways.

items.meaning: To express sincere gratitude for something.
items.example: Thanks for picking me up from the airport, I really appreciate it.
items.plain: Thanks for picking me up from the airport, I am very grateful.
items.note: Versatile for expressing thanks for a favour or kindness.

items.meaning: An informal way to encourage someone to stay in touch or visit again soon.
items.example: It was great catching up, don't be a stranger now!
items.plain: It was great catching up, please stay in touch and visit again soon!
items.note: Friendly and informal, used when parting ways with someone you want to see again.

items.meaning: A polite offer from a guest to contribute food or drink to a gathering.
items.example: What can I bring? I'll bring something to share for dessert.
items.plain: What can I bring? I will bring some food to share for dessert.
items.note: Standard polite offer when invited to someone's home.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly formal response to "thank you," meaning "you're welcome."
items.example: "Thanks for helping me move!" "It was my pleasure, glad I could assist."
items.plain: "Thanks for helping me move!" "You're welcome, glad I could assist."
items.note: More formal than "you're welcome," often used when you genuinely enjoyed helping.

items.meaning: A common greeting asking about someone's well-being since the last meeting.
items.example: Long time no see! How have you been since we last met?
items.plain: Long time no see! How are you doing since we last met?
items.note: Standard greeting for someone you haven't seen in a while.

items.text: What have you been up to
items.form: What have you been up to
items.meaning: An informal way to ask what someone has been doing recently.
items.example: It's been ages! What have you been up to since graduation?
items.plain: It's been ages! What have you been doing since graduation?
items.note: Very common and friendly for catching up.

items.meaning: An informal greeting used when meeting someone after a long period.
items.example: Oh, Sarah! Long time no see, how wonderful to bump into you!
items.plain: Oh, Sarah! I haven't seen you in a long time, how wonderful to bump into you!
items.note: Very common and friendly, often used as an opening remark.

items.meaning: An informal way to say a very long time has passed since the last meeting.
items.example: Wow, it's been ages since we last had coffee together.
items.plain: Wow, a very long time has passed since we last had coffee together.
items.note: Common and informal, expressing surprise or emphasis on the time passed.

items.meaning: To maintain communication with someone, usually informally.
items.example: It was great seeing you, let's promise to keep in touch more often.
items.plain: It was great seeing you, let's promise to communicate more often.
items.note: Common farewell, encouraging continued communication.

items.meaning: To provide someone with the latest information or details about something.
items.example: I heard you got a new job, fill me in on all the details!
items.plain: I heard you got a new job, tell me all the details!
items.note: Informal and direct, used when asking for an update.

items.meaning: An informal question asking for updates on someone's life.
items.example: So, what's new with you since we last spoke? Any exciting news?
items.plain: So, what has changed in your life since we last spoke? Any exciting news?
items.note: Common and friendly way to initiate a conversation about recent events.

items.meaning: A polite and friendly way to express enjoyment of an activity and suggest repeating it.
items.example: This dinner was fantastic, we should do this again very soon.
items.plain: This dinner was fantastic, we should meet up again very soon.
items.note: Common closing remark after a pleasant social interaction.

items.meaning: To express sadness or longing for someone's presence.
items.example: It's so good to finally see you, I've missed you a lot!
items.plain: It's so good to finally see you, I felt your absence a lot!
items.note: Sincere and warm, used with close friends or family.

items.meaning: A general, informal question asking about someone's overall situation or well-being.
items.example: Hey, how's everything going with your new project?
items.plain: Hey, how is your new project progressing?
items.note: Very common and versatile for starting a conversation or catching up.

items.meaning: A polite and indirect way to make a request or an invitation.
items.example: I was wondering if you'd be free for lunch next Tuesday.
items.plain: Would you be free for lunch next Tuesday?
items.note: Makes an invitation or request sound less demanding and more polite.

items.meaning: To express anticipation and excitement for a future event.
items.example: I'm looking forward to seeing you at the party on Saturday.
items.plain: I'm excited about seeing you at the party on Saturday.
items.note: Very common and positive expression of anticipation.

items.meaning: To ask someone to inform you about something.
items.example: If your plans change, please let me know so I can adjust.
items.plain: If your plans change, please inform me so I can adjust.
items.note: Direct and common request for information or updates.

items.meaning: To promise to respond or provide information at a later time.
items.example: I need to check my calendar, I'll get back to you about dinner plans.
items.plain: I need to check my calendar, I will respond to you about dinner plans later.
items.note: Common and polite way to defer a response.

items.meaning: To ask for a convenient time for a meeting or activity.
items.example: I'm free all afternoon, so what time works best for you to meet?
items.plain: I'm free all afternoon, so what time is most convenient for you to meet?
items.note: Direct and efficient way to coordinate schedules.

items.meaning: To state one's availability for a specific day or time.
items.example: I'm free on Friday evening if you want to grab a drink.
items.plain: I am available on Friday evening if you want to grab a drink.
items.note: Simple and clear way to communicate availability.

items.meaning: To explain one's unavailability due to a specific activity or commitment.
items.example: I'm busy with a family event this weekend, so I can't join.
items.plain: I have a family event this weekend, so I can't join.
items.note: Direct and common way to state a reason for being unavailable.

items.meaning: A polite way to decline an invitation while expressing a desire to accept.
items.example: I'd love to but I already have plans that night.
items.plain: I would really like to come but I already have plans that night.
items.note: Standard polite refusal, softening the rejection.

items.meaning: To express uncertainty about something, often related to availability or possibility.
items.example: I'm not sure if I can make it, I'll check my schedule and let you know.
items.plain: I don't know if I can make it, I'll check my schedule and let you know.
items.note: Useful for giving a tentative response when you need to confirm details.

items.meaning: An informal invitation to phone someone.
items.example: When you're free, just give me a call and we can arrange something.
items.plain: When you're free, just phone me and we can arrange something.
items.note: Common and friendly way to suggest initiating contact.

items.meaning: To visit someone informally and without a specific appointment.
items.example: If you're in the neighborhood, feel free to drop by for a coffee.
items.plain: If you're in the neighborhood, feel free to visit informally for a coffee.
items.note: Informal and casual invitation, implying no need for a formal plan.

items.meaning: Similar to "drop by," to make a quick, informal visit.
items.example: I'm just at home, why don't you pop over for a quick chat?
items.plain: I'm just at home, why don't you come over quickly for a chat?
items.note: Very informal, often implies a short visit. More common in British English.

items.meaning: To make a quick, informal visit, often on the way to somewhere else.
items.example: I'll swing by your place after work to pick up the books.
items.plain: I'll visit your place quickly after work to pick up the books.
items.note: Informal, implies a brief stop.

items.meaning: To confirm one's attendance at an event or meeting.
items.example: Thanks for the invitation to the concert, I'll be there for sure!
items.plain: Thanks for the invitation to the concert, I will definitely attend!
items.note: Simple and direct confirmation of attendance.

items.meaning: To express strong excitement and eagerness for a future event or activity.
items.example: I can't wait to see you all at the reunion next month!
items.plain: I am very excited to see you all at the reunion next month!
items.note: Very common and enthusiastic expression of anticipation.

items.meaning: A polite and enthusiastic way to suggest an activity or meeting.
items.example: It would be great to catch up properly soon, maybe over dinner.
items.plain: It would be very nice to catch up properly soon, maybe over dinner.
items.note: Friendly and positive way to make a suggestion.

items.text: I'm really looking forward to it
items.form: I'm really looking forward to it
items.meaning: To express strong anticipation and excitement for a specific event.
items.example: Thanks for inviting me to the party, I'm really looking forward to it!
items.plain: Thanks for inviting me to the party, I am very excited about it!
items.note: Common and enthusiastic response when accepting an invitation.

items.meaning: A polite and gentle way to say "no" or decline something.
items.example: "Are you free for coffee tomorrow?" "I'm afraid not, I have an early meeting."
items.plain: "Are you free for coffee tomorrow?" "No, I have an early meeting."
items.note: Softer than a direct "no," often used when declining.

items.meaning: A polite and gentle way to say "yes" to something undesirable or unfortunate.
items.example: "Is the party cancelled?" "I'm afraid so, the host is unwell."
items.plain: "Is the party cancelled?" "Yes, the host is unwell."
items.note: Used to confirm something negative or unwelcome.

items.meaning: To promise to provide updates or information as it becomes available.
items.example: I'm still waiting for confirmation, but I'll keep you posted on the details.
items.plain: I'm still waiting for confirmation, but I will give you updates on the details.
items.note: Common and useful for ongoing plans or uncertain situations.

items.meaning: A suggestion to arrange a specific time and activity to meet.
items.example: It's been too long, let's make a plan to get together next month.
items.plain: It's been too long, let's arrange a specific time to get together next month.
items.note: Friendly and proactive way to initiate concrete plans.

items.meaning: To express willingness and pleasure in doing something.
items.example: I'm happy to host the next book club meeting at my place.
items.plain: I am willing to host the next book club meeting at my place.
items.note: Polite and positive way to offer help or volunteer.

items.text: I'm not really feeling up to it
items.form: I'm not really feeling up to it
items.meaning: To express a lack of energy or desire to do something, often due to tiredness or illness.
items.example: Thanks for the invite, but I'm not really feeling up to it tonight.
items.plain: Thanks for the invite, but I don't have the energy or desire to go tonight.
items.note: Polite and common way to decline due to not feeling well or being tired.

items.meaning: To briefly leave one's current location, usually for a short errand.
items.example: I'm just popping out to the shop, I'll be back in ten minutes.
items.plain: I'm just leaving briefly to go to the shop, I'll be back in ten minutes.
items.note: Informal, implies a quick, temporary departure. More common in British English.

items.meaning: To inform someone that you are leaving briefly and will return very soon.
items.example: Excuse me for a moment, I'll be right back after I grab a drink.
items.plain: Excuse me for a moment, I will return very soon after I grab a drink.
items.note: Common phrase for a very short, temporary absence.

items.meaning: To inform someone that you will arrive slightly after the scheduled time.
items.example: Sorry, I'm running a bit late, I'll be there in about ten minutes.
items.plain: Sorry, I will arrive a little after the scheduled time, I'll be there in about ten minutes.
items.note: Common and polite way to inform someone of a slight delay.

items.meaning: To inform someone that you have departed and are traveling to the destination.
items.example: Just leaving now, I'm on my way to your place.
items.plain: Just leaving now, I am traveling to your place.
items.note: Common update when heading to a meeting or event.

items.meaning: A confirmation that one will meet someone at a specified location.
items.example: Okay, great! I'll see you there at 7 PM then.
items.plain: Okay, great! I will meet you at that location at 7 PM then.
items.note: Simple and common way to confirm meeting arrangements.

items.meaning: To ask for a suggested time when someone proposes an activity.
items.example: That sounds fun! What time are you thinking for the movie?
items.plain: That sounds fun! What time do you suggest for the movie?
items.note: Friendly way to prompt for more specific details about a plan.

items.meaning: To indicate that one is willing to consider different ideas or plans.
items.example: I'm not sure what to do this weekend, I'm open to suggestions.
items.plain: I'm not sure what to do this weekend, I am willing to consider different ideas.
items.note: Useful when you want input from others for planning.

items.meaning: To indicate that one can adapt to different times or arrangements.
items.example: Any day next week works for me, I'm flexible.
items.plain: Any day next week works for me, I can adapt to different times.
items.note: Simple and clear way to communicate adaptability in scheduling.

items.meaning: To state that one needs to consult their schedule before confirming availability.
items.example: That sounds interesting, I'll check my calendar and get back to you.
items.plain: That sounds interesting, I will look at my schedule and respond to you.
items.note: Common and polite way to give a tentative response.

items.meaning: To promise to provide a definite answer at a subsequent time.
items.example: I'm not sure about Saturday yet, I'll confirm later tonight.
items.plain: I'm not sure about Saturday yet, I will give a definite answer later tonight.
items.note: Useful when you need time to finalize plans.

items.meaning: To indicate that one is on the verge of doing something.
items.example: I'm just about to leave for the restaurant, see you soon!
items.plain: I am going to leave for the restaurant very soon, see you soon!
items.note: Common for giving a real-time update on one's immediate actions.

items.meaning: To announce that one is leaving a place.
items.example: Okay, I'm heading out now, see you at the cinema.
items.plain: Okay, I am leaving now, see you at the cinema.
items.note: Informal way to announce departure.

items.meaning: To express what one is seeking or hoping to find, often for social plans.
items.example: I'm looking for something fun to do this weekend, any ideas?
items.plain: I want to find something fun to do this weekend, any ideas?
items.note: Useful for initiating plans when you don't have a specific idea.

items.meaning: To express willingness or enthusiasm to participate in an activity.
items.example: A game of tennis this afternoon? Yeah, I'm up for it!
items.plain: A game of tennis this afternoon? Yes, I am willing to do it!
items.note: Informal and enthusiastic way to agree to an activity.

items.meaning: To express a lack of interest or preference for a particular activity.
items.example: I'm not really into crowded bars, maybe we could try a quiet cafe instead.
items.plain: I don't really like crowded bars, maybe we could try a quiet cafe instead.
items.note: Polite way to decline or suggest an alternative based on preference.

items.meaning: An informal way to say "I'll contact you" or "I'll call you."
items.example: When I get home, I'll give you a shout to finalize our plans.
items.plain: When I get home, I will contact you to finalize our plans.
items.note: Very informal, common in British English.

items.meaning: To promise to communicate with someone soon.
items.example: It was great meeting you, I'll be in touch about that project next week.
items.plain: It was great meeting you, I will contact you about that project next week.
items.note: Standard and polite way to end a conversation with a promise of future contact.

items.meaning: An informal way to ask about someone's plans, often to suggest an activity.
items.example: Are you doing anything this evening? I was thinking of going to the cinema.
items.plain: Do you have plans this evening? I was thinking of going to the cinema.
items.note: Common and friendly way to initiate plans or check availability.

items.meaning: To introduce a suggestion or idea for an activity.
items.example: I was thinking of having a small get-together at my place on Friday.
items.plain: I had the idea of having a small get-together at my place on Friday.
items.note: Polite and common way to propose an activity or plan.

items.meaning: An informal British English way to ask what someone would like to do or eat.
items.example: We're going out for dinner, what do you fancy eating tonight?
items.plain: We're going out for dinner, what would you like to eat tonight?
items.note: Very informal, primarily British English. Used to ask for preferences.

items.meaning: To indicate that one has no strong preference and is happy with any choice.
items.example: Pizza or pasta? I'm easy, whatever you prefer.
items.plain: Pizza or pasta? I have no strong preference, whatever you prefer.
items.note: Informal. Means 'I don't mind' or 'I'm flexible'.

items.meaning: To indicate a lack of preference or concern about a choice.
items.example: Which movie should we watch? I'm not bothered, you choose.
items.plain: Which movie should we watch? I don't care, you choose.
items.note: Informal, often British English. Can sound slightly indifferent if tone is flat.

items.meaning: To express willingness to do any activity suggested.
items.example: I'm free this weekend, I'm up for anything fun you have in mind.
items.plain: I'm free this weekend, I am willing to do any fun activity you have in mind.
items.note: Enthusiastic and informal way to show flexibility and openness to ideas.

items.text: I'm not really in the mood for
items.form: I'm not really in the mood for
items.meaning: To express a lack of desire for a particular activity or type of food.
items.example: I'm not really in the mood for cooking tonight, let's order takeout.
items.plain: I don't really want to cook tonight, let's order takeout.
items.note: Polite way to express a current preference or lack thereof.

items.meaning: To offer to pay for someone's meal, drink, or activity.
items.example: It's your birthday, so I'll treat you to dinner tonight.
items.plain: It's your birthday, so I will pay for your dinner tonight.
items.note: Friendly and generous offer, common for special occasions or as a thank you.

items.meaning: An informal way to say that one will pay for something.
items.example: Don't worry about the bill, it's on me tonight.
items.plain: Don't worry about the bill, I will pay for it tonight.
items.note: Informal and friendly way to offer to pay, often for a round of drinks or a meal.

items.meaning: An informal way to say that one is paying for something as a gift.
items.example: Let me get this coffee, my treat!
items.plain: Let me get this coffee, I am paying for it as a gift!
items.note: Friendly and informal, often used for smaller gestures like coffee or a snack.

items.meaning: A polite offer to fetch a drink or food for a guest.
items.example: Please sit down, can I get you anything to drink?
items.plain: Please sit down, would you like me to bring you anything to drink?
items.note: Standard hospitable offer to guests in one's home.

items.meaning: A polite way to decline an offer of food or drink.
items.example: Would you like another slice of cake? No, I'm good thanks.
items.plain: Would you like another slice of cake? No, I've had enough, thank you.
items.note: Common and polite refusal, indicating satisfaction or no need.

items.meaning: To indicate that one has everything needed or is ready.
items.example: Are you ready to go? Yes, I'm all set.
items.plain: Are you ready to go? Yes, I have everything I need.
items.note: Versatile, can mean 'I'm ready' or 'I have enough' (e.g., food/drink).

items.meaning: An informal way to say one has eaten too much and is very full.
items.example: That was delicious, but I'm stuffed, I couldn't eat another bite.
items.plain: That was delicious, but I am very full, I couldn't eat another bite.
items.note: Informal and common after a large meal. Friendly.

items.meaning: An informal and exaggerated way to say one is very hungry.
items.example: What time is dinner? I'm starving, I haven't eaten all day!
items.plain: What time is dinner? I am very hungry, I haven't eaten all day!
items.note: Informal and common, used to express extreme hunger.

items.meaning: An informal and humorous way to say one is extremely hungry.
items.example: I've been working all day, I could eat a horse right now!
items.plain: I've been working all day, I am extremely hungry right now!
items.note: Informal and humorous exaggeration of hunger. Not literal.

items.meaning: An informal way to say one is very thirsty.
items.example: It's so hot today, I'm parched, I need a big glass of water.
items.plain: It's so hot today, I am very thirsty, I need a big glass of water.
items.note: Informal, often used after physical activity or in hot weather.

items.meaning: An informal British English way to say one is extremely tired.
items.example: I had a terrible night's sleep, I'm shattered today.
items.plain: I had a terrible night's sleep, I am extremely tired today.
items.note: Very informal, primarily British English. Stronger than 'knackered'.

items.meaning: An informal way to say one is feeling excited and energetic.
items.example: I just got great news, I'm buzzing with excitement!
items.plain: I just got great news, I am feeling very excited and energetic!
items.note: Informal, often used after good news or a stimulating event.

items.text: I'm feeling a bit under the weather
items.form: I'm feeling a bit under the weather
items.meaning: A polite way to say one is feeling slightly unwell or sick.
items.example: I'm feeling a bit under the weather, so I might skip the party tonight.
items.plain: I am feeling slightly unwell, so I might skip the party tonight.
items.note: Common and polite way to explain mild illness without going into detail.

items.meaning: To indicate that one is not feeling as well or energetic as usual.
items.example: I'm not feeling myself today, I think I'll just stay home and rest.
items.plain: I am not feeling as well or energetic as usual today, I think I'll just stay home.
items.note: Polite way to express feeling unwell or out of sorts.

items.meaning: To express enjoyment of an event or activity.
items.example: Thank you for inviting me, I'm having a great time at your party!
items.plain: Thank you for inviting me, I am really enjoying myself at your party!
items.note: Common and positive expression of enjoyment, often said to a host.

items.text: I'm glad you could make it
items.form: I'm glad you could make it
items.meaning: A polite expression of pleasure that someone was able to attend.
items.example: Oh, you're here! I'm glad you could make it to the gathering.
items.plain: Oh, you're here! I am pleased you were able to attend the gathering.
items.note: Common and welcoming phrase from a host to a guest.

items.text: It was good to see you
items.form: It was good to see you
items.meaning: A polite and friendly farewell, expressing enjoyment of someone's company.
items.example: Right, I must be off. It was good to see you again!
items.plain: Right, I must be off. I enjoyed seeing you again!
items.note: Common and friendly closing remark when parting ways.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly formal way to say one enjoyed an interaction or meeting.
items.example: Thank you for the insightful conversation, it was a pleasure meeting you.
items.plain: Thank you for the insightful conversation, I enjoyed meeting you.
items.note: Polite and slightly formal, often used when meeting someone new.

items.meaning: A polite offer to accompany a guest to the door when they are leaving.
items.example: It's getting late, I'll walk you out to your car.
items.plain: It's getting late, I will accompany you to your car.
items.note: Hospitable gesture from a host to a departing guest.

items.meaning: A polite way for a guest to indicate they can leave without being accompanied.
items.example: Don't worry, I'll see myself out, you stay warm inside.
items.plain: Don't worry, I can leave by myself, you stay warm inside.
items.note: Polite and considerate, used by a guest to avoid inconveniencing the host.

items.meaning: An offer to give a tour of a place, often one's home or a new location.
items.example: Welcome to my new apartment, I'll show you around.
items.plain: Welcome to my new apartment, I will give you a tour.
items.note: Common hospitable offer when guests arrive at a new place.

items.meaning: An offer to present someone to another person or group.
items.example: Come on in, I'll introduce you to everyone at the party.
items.plain: Come on in, I will present you to everyone at the party.
items.note: Common and friendly offer when bringing someone new to a social gathering.

items.meaning: An informal way to say "I'll see you later" or "I'll talk to you later."
items.example: I need to grab another drink, I'll catch you later!
items.plain: I need to grab another drink, I will see you again later!
items.note: Very informal, used when temporarily parting ways at an event.

items.meaning: To promise to communicate with someone in the near future.
items.example: It was great chatting, I'll be in touch soon about that project.
items.plain: It was great chatting, I will contact you in the near future about that project.
items.note: Standard and polite way to end a conversation with a promise of future contact.

items.meaning: An informal British English way to say "I'll call you."
items.example: I'll give you a ring tomorrow to confirm the details.
items.plain: I will call you tomorrow to confirm the details.
items.note: Informal, primarily British English. Means 'I'll phone you'.

items.meaning: An informal way to say "I'll send you a message" or "I'll write to you."
items.example: I'll drop you a line with the address later today.
items.plain: I will send you a message with the address later today.
items.note: Informal, can refer to an email, text, or short note.

items.meaning: To promise to send a text message to someone.
items.example: I'll text you when I'm on my way to the restaurant.
items.plain: I will send you a text message when I'm on my way to the restaurant.
items.note: Very common and direct way to promise a text message.

items.meaning: To promise to send a message to someone, often via an app or social media.
items.example: I'll message you the details for the event later.
items.plain: I will send you a message with the details for the event later.
items.note: Common and versatile, covers various digital messaging platforms.
